Järva is notable for both its high levels of diversity and persistent socioeconomic and safety challenges. In several areas the distribution of foreign-born residents range between 70–90%, particularly in the central and northern neighborhoods ([Stockholm Stad, 2024](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B77)). These areas face structural inequality and lower perceived safety than the city average. Media attention has intensified in recent years due to gang-related violence, including shootings and bombings ([Wall et al., 2024](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B84)). While total crime rates and certain categories such as theft have decreased and remained below the city average, violent crime has instead increased ([Brå, 2025](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B8)). Swedish police have designated several neighborhoods within Järva (Husby, Rinkeby/ Tensta) as “_particularly vulnerable areas” (“särskilt utsatta områden”_), marked by significant challenges with crime, socioeconomic disadvantage, and trust and participation in institutions ([NOA, 2017](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B61)). While the label reflects structural disadvantage, it has also reinforced long-standing territorial stigma. Since the 1970s, neighborhoods in Järva have been portrayed as dirty, disorderly, and plagued by substance abuse and crime – problems increasingly attributed to its immigrant population ([Ericsson et al., 2002](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B20)).

In response, Järva has become a key focus of Stockholm’s urban development strategy, emphasizing new housing, jobs, infrastructure, and safer public spaces ([Stockholm Stad, 2025](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B78)). Local initiatives have focused on disrupting drug markets and fostering place-based collaboration (“_platssamverkan_”) among authorities and locals in particularly vulnerable areas. Introduced in 2019, the “Three-phase” model coordinates police, social services, and the Swedish Prison and Probation Service to combat rising gun violence in Järva and has been linked to a relative decline in shootings compared to the rest of Stockholm County ([Wall et al., 2024](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B84)). Yet other interventions, such as the temporary stop-and-frisk-zones, have garnered much criticism for being discriminatory and largely ineffective in reducing gang crime ([Moreno & Mattison, 2024](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B60)).

### Methodology

#### Survey of locals and outsiders

A web survey was designed to capture safety perceptions of Järva through three lenses: the deep local knowledge of residents, the frequent but transitory experiences of commuters and other visitors, and the limited experience and second-hand knowledge of non-visitors. To achieve this, three tailored questionnaires were created using _Maptionnaire_ ([Mapita, 2025](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B89)), an interactive online survey platform that integrates various question types with mapping functionalities. By allowing respondents to anchor perceptions to specific locations, the survey tool helps generate more spatially detailed data on fear – addressing a key limitation in the literature on micro-places of fear ([Solymosi et al., 2020](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B75)). In this study, it also offers insight into respondents’ mobility patterns and the geography of both fear and place attachment. These types of approaches commonly fall under the term _public participatory geographic information systems_ (PPGIS), which in fear research have involved both pen-and-paper map sketching ([Curtis et al., 2014](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B14)) and digital mapping tools and smartphones ([Kronkvist & Engström, 2020](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B48); [Kyttä et al., 2014](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B50); [Solymosi et al., 2020](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B75)). These methods have proven useful for identifying both spatial clusters of unsafe places and the place typologies of fear and safety ([Ceccato & Snickars, 2000](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B11); [Kyttä et al., 2014](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B50); [Pánek et al., 2019](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B65); [Guldåker et al., 2024](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B29)).

The surveys targeting residents and frequent visitors (defined as the _locals_ of Järva) were distributed via a single shared link, promoted through multiple channels. This included online distribution via the Järva district administration, university mailing lists, and local companies and organizations, but also physical distribution via QR-code posters at libraries, malls, community spaces, and seasonal events. The survey link led to a landing page with two clearly labeled options (in both Swedish and English): “Live in Järva? Click here!” and “Work in and/or visit Järva often? Click here!”, directing respondents to the appropriate version of the questionnaire. Non-visitors (defined as the _outsiders_ of Järva) were targeted separately, mainly through the Stockholm City official website and social media. Although the survey links were technically open to anyone, responses were reviewed during data cleaning to ensure alignment with the intended respondent group. Only one misclassified entry was found based on open-text responses indicating inconsistent residence information, and was therefore removed. Conducted between June 2023 and January 2024, the survey collected 592 valid responses across the three questionnaires, including 152 Järva residents, 48 commuters/visitors, and 392 non-visitors.

All three questionnaires recorded background information, including age, gender, origin (Swedish/foreign background), educational attainment, sexuality, and ability status. [Table 1](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#T1) provides an overview of the respondent distribution.

The questionnaires for residents and frequent visitors were essentially identical, apart from minor differences in phrasing. Locals were asked about their overall perception of Järva, places they liked or avoided due to safety concerns, past victimization, willingness to reside in the area, and suggestions for improvement. Outsiders received similar questions but, naturally, fewer about direct experiences. They first described their own neighborhood before sharing their perceptions of Järva. Additionally, one question assessed outsiders’ potential perceptual bias linked to Järva’s built environment using Google Street View images. A total of 12 Street View images were selected—six from locations within Järva and six from outside. Each set of six was evenly split between images previously rated as high- or low-safety in a prior Stockholm study, based on a deep learning analysis of urban imagery trained on city-wide survey responses (for more detail see [Abraham et al., 2025](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B2); [Kang et al., 2023](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B43)). Respondents were asked to “Choose 4 images that you think are typical environments of Järva,” and selections were recorded for each image.

#### Statistical procedure and data processing

While the Maptionnaire platform provides an internal analysis tool for the results, the survey datasets were imported to the statistical software package IBM SPSS Statistics (version 28.0), where most of the analysis was undertaken.

Due to the study’s design, questionnaires, and respondent group definitions, descriptive analyses for locals and outsiders were conducted separately. Both quantitative and qualitative methods were used to characterize the datasets. Cross-tabulations and chi-square tests were employed to identify significant differences in respondent characteristics, with an additional chi-square analysis among outsiders to explore variation in image-based safety perceptions of Järva. A marginal significance threshold of 10% was used, with higher levels reported in tables and text. Open-text responses were analyzed to contextualize the findings. Spatial data were processed in QGIS, including mapped responses of places in Järva locals liked, felt safe or unsafe in, or viewed as unsafe but unavoidable. To assess spatial patterns, we used Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) to visualize concentrations of responses and Average Nearest Neighbor (ANN) analysis to evaluate their statistical significance. KDE is a well-established method for point-pattern analysis that has been widely applied to study both crime ([Chainey et al., 2008](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B12); [Eck et al., 2005](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B17)) and fear of crime ([Guldåker et al., 2024](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B29)).

Binomial regression was used to examine how respondent characteristics influenced safety perceptions of Järva, with locals and outsiders analyzed together. Two models were developed to assess safety perceptions. As locals by definition have first-hand, time-specific experiences of Järva, they were asked, “Is Järva a safe area...”, with follow-up prompts for daytime and nighttime, using a Likert scale from 5 (“Very safe”) to 1 (“Very unsafe”). Outsiders, having limited firsthand experience, were instead asked: “What is your idea of the safety in Järva?”, using the same Likert scale but without time-specific prompts. While this difference in operationalization may affect comparability, it was necessary to ensure valid and meaningful responses across groups. To align the data, values 1 and 2 (“Very unsafe” and “Unsafe”) were recoded as 1, and all others as 0. The two models combined outsider assessments with locals’ daytime and nighttime responses, respectively – referred to as “Unsafe Perception of Järva (Day)” and “Unsafe Perception of Järva (Night), with the caveat that outsider assessments are not time-specific.

The third and final model used willingness to reside in Järva as the dependent variable, with the question framed differently for residents and non-residents. Residents were asked, “If you had the opportunity, would you choose to live elsewhere than in Järva?”, with response options: “Yes, due to poor safety,” “Yes, but due to other reasons,” and “No.” Non-residents were asked, “If you had the opportunity, would you choose to live in Järva?”, with corresponding response options: “No, due to poor safety,” “No, due to other reasons,” and “Yes.” Responses indicating unwillingness to reside in Järva due to poor safety were coded as 1, while all other responses were coded as 0.

The key variable in all three models was familiarity of Järva, represented by dummy variables indicating if the respondent was a resident (used as the reference category), frequent visitor, outsider who had visited the neighborhood at least once, outsider who had only heard of the area, and an outsider who had never heard of Järva. Control variables included the background characteristics in [Table 1](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#T1), as well as previous history of victimization and distrust in police.

Results
-------

### ‘Local’ perceptions of Järva

#### Chi-square analysis

In total, the local respondents included 160 residents and 50 visitors. [Table 2](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#T2) presents cross-tabulation results on safety perceptions and willingness to reside in Järva, broken down by group and significant background variables. Daytime perceptions of Järva are largely positive, with 72% of locals considering it “Safe” to “Very Safe” and 15% labeling it “Unsafe/Very Unsafe”. While residents reported feeling safer than visitors (76% vs. 63%), the difference was not statistically significant. Similarly, age, gender, sexuality, place of birth, ability status, education, trust in police, and prior victimization had no significant impact on daytime safety perceptions.

At night, perceptions shift drastically, with only 30% feeling safe and 37% reporting Järva as unsafe (N=137). Half of the visitors felt unsafe at night compared to 36% of residents, but this difference was again not statistically significant. The only notable background factor was place of birth, where foreign-born respondents were marginally more likely to perceive Järva as unsafe at night than Swedish-born respondents (53% vs. 36%, p <0.1). Relatedly, 17% of locals reported feeling unsafe due to their heritage/origin, though no significant differences emerged between Swedish and foreign-born groups. Neither length of residency nor work/school tenure significantly influenced safety perceptions at any time of day. Despite poorer nighttime safety perceptions, only 14% of respondents wanted to move due to safety concerns, while 52% cited other reasons such as proximity to the city center, job opportunities, education, and services. Visitors, by contrast, seem more influenced by safety concerns, with a significantly larger share (36%, p<0.05) unwilling to move to Järva specifically due to safety reasons.

#### Typology and concentration of (un)safe places in Järva

The safety conditions in Järva significantly influence residents’ mobility and relationship with places. [Figure 2](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#F2) maps locations identified by locals as safe, enjoyable, unsafe, or unsafe but unavoidable. Overall, visitors primarily mapped locations in northern Järva, particularly Kista, Husby, and Akalla, while residents’ responses were more evenly distributed. Malls and squares featured prominently among perceived safe places. Kista Mall was frequently cited, attributed to the presence of ‘many eyes and guards’. Similarly, in southern Järva, many locations surrounding Spånga square were seen as safe, due to being “large open space with a lot of movement”, with people always present and amenities like shops and restaurants. In central Järva, larger green spaces, meadows, and scenic viewpoints were commonly perceived as safe areas, with some respondents reporting they “always feel safe in nature” while others noted that this was less true during night. Safety was also associated with purposeful movement, where people “have a reason” to be in the area, contrasting it with locations linked to drug activity. Locations enjoyed for leisure largely overlapped with safe places but were more numerous ([Figure 2b](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#F2)). However, enjoyment was driven less by safety and more by visual appeal, vibrancy, and available activities ([Figure 3a](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#F3)).

Unsafe locations were more unevenly distributed but showed consistent patterns. Key areas of concern include transportation hubs in northern Järva (e.g. Kista bus square, Husby metro), as well as neighborhood centers in central Järva, particularly Rinkeby and Tensta Centrum ([Figures 3c and 3d](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#F3)). This perception is especially pronounced at night ([Figure 2d](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#F2)). However, several areas, including Rinkeby Centrum and sections of Tensta, Husby, and Kista, are seen as unsafe both during the day and at night. When asked “For the place you feel is the most unsafe, please describe why” ([Figure 3b](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#F3)), the majority (69%) cited knowledge or reports of past crimes at the locations, while a smaller share (12%) had personally been victimized there. Built environment factors were cited by 44%, with concerns about poor lighting, lack of maintenance, or a deserted feel. Additionally, 29% attributed their concerns to antisocial behavior, such as public alcohol or drug use, aggressive begging, and perceived stalking. Open-text responses emphasized certain issues, particularly pointing out the reputations of specific locations and known crime events, often related to drug use/dealing and shootings. There were also other safety concerns raised, including accident risks near a large construction site, heavily trafficked and high-speed roads, as well as two mentions of the heavy presence of ticket controllers at subway stations, which made one respondent feel “very uneasy”.

More than two in five respondents (42%) reported actively avoiding certain places in Järva due to safety concerns, while 30% identified places they considered unsafe but felt they could not avoid (N=105). The bus transit hub near Kista Mall was most frequently mentioned, particularly by visitors. Several mapped locations also aligned with other transit hubs in Järva, while central Järva appeared largely free from both unsafe and unavoidable places during the day ([Figure 2e](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#F2)).

To identify and visualize statistically significant spatial clustering, we applied both Average Nearest Neighbor (ANN) analysis and Kernel Density Estimation (KDE). The ANN-results confirm significant clustering (z < −1.96) for all perception types except for unavoidable unsafe places (z = −1.02), likely due to the smaller sample size. [Table 3](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#T3) summarizes the ANN statistics for the significant categories. The KDE-maps ([Figure 4](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#F4)) reinforce earlier findings: liked and safe places ([Figures 5a–b](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#F5)) cluster primarily in northern Järva, with Kista emerging as the dominant hotspot. In contrast, perceived unsafe areas show intense hotspots around the centrums of Kista and Rinkeby during the day, while during the night, concentrations around Tensta and Husby also appear – though these are comparably slightly more dispersed throughout the neighborhood.

### ‘Outsider’ perceptions of Järva

Among outsider respondents (N=392), the majority had some familiarity with Järva: two-thirds had visited once or twice, one-fifth had never visited but knew of it, and about one in ten had never heard of Järva. Additionally, 5% knew someone who had been a victim of crime in Järva. [Table 4](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#T4) shows chi-square results on safety perceptions and residence preferences among outsiders, based on familiarity and background variables that showed significant associations. The survey further accentuates Järva’s stigmatization, as 44% of outsiders perceived it as “Unsafe” or “Very Unsafe,” while only 11% considered it “Safe” or “Very Safe.” Familiarity significantly influenced perceptions (p = 0.01), with 47% of those who had visited Järva once viewing it as unsafe, compared to 70% of those who had only heard of it. However, similar to local respondents, age, gender, and other individual characteristics showed no significant differences in safety perceptions.

In contrast, when asked what they felt about their own neighborhood, 69% reported feeling safe to very safe, while 12% felt unsafe or very unsafe. As expected, no notable differences emerged between levels of familiarity with Järva; however, gender differences were significant, with men feeling safer than women (74% vs. 61%, p < 0.001). Swedish-born respondents also perceived their neighborhoods as safe significantly more often than foreign-born respondents (72.5% vs. 60.4%, p = 0.04). When asked about moving to Järva, 40% (N=227) declined due to safety concerns, while half cited other reasons, mainly the area’s remoteness and socioeconomic challenges. Despite this, 53% expressed willingness to visit, and 31% were open to working in the area.

Beyond safety perceptions, outsiders’ broader associations with Järva were also examined. When asked “When you think of Järva, which of these words do you think of?”, the most selected responses were “Segregated” (59%), “Dangerous” (41%), and “Boring” (38%). Only 6% considered the area attractive, though many acknowledged its diversity and role as a technology hub in Stockholm. In open-text responses, crime, particularly shootings and gang violence, was frequently mentioned. Some respondents linked crime to immigration, viewing diversity negatively. Conversely, a few attributed Järva’s challenges to socioeconomic oppression, racism, and media scapegoating. Perceptions of Järva’s urban environment and infrastructure were mixed. While many described it as a “slum,” “ghetto,” underdeveloped, or lacking identity, others highlighted its abundant green spaces and natural areas. Some outsiders also recognized intra-area contrasts, viewing Kista and Spånga more favorably than Rinkeby and Tensta.

To further examine how the built environment influences perceptions of Järva, respondents were asked to select four Street View images (out of 12) they believed were typical of Järva ([Figure 5](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#F5)). The images depicted various locations across Stockholm, with only six actually showing environments in Järva. As outlined in the methodology, these images were pre-classified by perceived safety, with “unsafe” images generally showing disorder, graffiti, and desolation, while “safe” images featured well-maintained, vibrant spaces with greenery. The results once again indicate that stigmatization affects our sensory understanding of environments. While respondents correctly identified Järva images most of the time, a clear bias emerged in non-Järva selections. Images depicting safe environments outside Järva were ignored more often than chosen (51% not selected), whereas non-Järva images with low safety ratings were incorrectly identified as Järva 82% of the time. These differences were statistically significant (χ²(3, N=326) = 91.7, p < 0.001), reinforcing the presence of a strong visual bias that associates Järva with unsafe environments—regardless of whether the images actually depict the area.

Model 1 has the strongest explanatory power, explaining nearly 30% of the variance in perceived safety (Nagelkerke R 2 = 0.29). Familiarity with Järva emerges as a key determinant of both safety perceptions and willingness to reside in the area, with several categories of familiarity showing highly significant effects (p < 0.01) across all models. Notably, when these variables are removed, the Nagelkerke R2 reduces to 0.03-0.04 across the models, suggesting that familiarity alone accounts for the vast majority of the explanatory value.

When comparing with daytime perceptions (Model 1), only outsiders exhibit significantly different safety perceptions compared to residents. Single-visit outsiders are 6.7 times more likely to perceive Järva as unsafe, while those with only secondhand knowledge hold the most negative perceptions, being nearly 26 times more likely to consider it unsafe. In contrast, frequent visitors and individuals who have never heard of Järva show no evidence of perceiving safety differently than residents, at least during daytime. In Model 2, the dynamics shift, as frequent visitors become significantly more likely to see Järva as unsafe at night, four times as likely compared to residents. However, those with secondhand knowledge remain the most negative, being over eight times more likely than residents to perceive the area as unsafe. These same three categories of familiarity are also significantly associated with unwillingness to reside in Järva, increasing the likelihood between five to nearly seven times compared to residents.

While the direction and significance of the effects are clear, the 95% confidence intervals (CIs) suggest cautious interpretation of the odds ratios, especially when comparing the familiarity levels. For instance, those who have only heard of Järva show a notably high odds ratio in Model 1 (OR = 25.78), yet its wide CI (9.19–72.31) overlaps with that of single-visit outsiders (CI = 3.17–14.30), indicating their effects may not be statistically different. To assess whether these odds ratios were truly distinct, likelihood ratio tests were conducted, comparing full models with models where familiarity categories were pairwise combined. The results confirmed that single-visit outsiders and those with secondhand knowledge of Järva had significantly different effects in Models 1 and 2, but not in Model 3. Frequent visitors differed significantly from the outsider groups only in Model 1, where the variable itself was not significant. In Models 2 and 3, no significant differences emerged between frequent visitors and outsiders, suggesting that at night and in residency decisions, the impact of familiarity is less sharply differentiated.

While individual relationships with Järva play a significant role in shaping perceptions, few other background characteristics show significant effects. Prior crime victimization was significantly associated with negative perceptions and reluctance to live in Järva, doubling the likelihood compared to non-victims in all three models. Younger respondents (under 30 years) were twice as likely to perceive Järva negatively during the day and resist living there, though their nighttime concerns are only marginally significant (75% more likely, p<0.1). Female respondents were on the margin of having a weak significant association with poor nighttime perceptions (p=0.11), but otherwise, gender and other background variables do not appear to be significant predictors of perceptions of Järva in either of the models.

Discussion
----------

In this paper, we explored how perceptions of residents and frequent visitors (locals) and non-visitors (outsiders) are shaped by local knowledge, transitory experiences, and secondhand information. We attempt to unravel these relationships by investigating locals and outsiders of Järva both separately and simultaneously, combining qualitative analysis with descriptive, spatial, and inferential statistics. Our findings highlight the dynamic nature of safety perceptions, as well as patterns of stigma and bias towards Järva, while also hinting at more complex relationships. The results make several methodological and theoretical research contributions.

For one, the findings support the relevancy of incorporating user positionality, emphasizing how differences in experiential knowledge and familiarity shape place perceptions. Both the descriptive analysis and the regression model show that outsiders had a significantly more negative view of Järva than locals, while often assessing their own neighborhood as safe. This finding aligns with previous research ([Lorenc et al., 2013](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B54); [Kronkvist, 2022](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B46)), while this study further builds upon it by demonstrating that different levels of place familiarity have a significant effect even between non-residential place-users. The results suggest that even smaller increases in experiential knowledge, such as the difference in only hearing of a place versus physically visiting it at least once, may be enough to improve safety perceptions and combat stigma significantly. At the same time, the results reveal that both residents and frequent visitors experience variations in perceived safety that are temporally dependent. Both residents and visitors largely viewed Järva as safe during the day, contrasting with the district’s broader reputation. However, the regression results reveal that visitors express more negative perceptions of safety at night than residents. While the effect on perceived safety of nighttime factors is well documented ([Blöbaum & Hunecke, 2005](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B3); [Himschoot et al., 2024](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B35)), previous research on place attachment and stigma may help explain the resident-visitor discrepancy ([Haynes et al., 2013](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B33); [Ilovan & Markuszewska, 2022](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B38)). While residents can develop strong emotional attachments that buffer against safety concerns, even to poorly reputed neighborhoods, non-residents, with weak (or non-existent) neighborhood bonds, are more susceptible to negative reputations ([Ilovan & Markuszewska, 2022](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B38)). The negative nighttime perceptions of visitors despite their experience with Järva suggest that general familiarity alone does not ensure a sense of safety. Familiar places may also carry negative associations ([Lupton, 1999](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B57)). In order to get home, visitors tend to congregate around transport stations in the evening, locations often noted as sources of fear, particularly at night (for a review, see [Ceccato et al., 2022](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B10)). Concerns that arise from these spaces could potentially be normalized by residents, while frequent visitors may not have developed a strong enough attachment to disregard them. This aligns with the dispositional and situational safety dynamic ([Gabriel & Greve, 2003](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B26)), where residents’ perceptions can be said to be more stable and rooted in long-term attachment and daily routines, while visitors’ perceptions are more situational, influenced by the specific environments they navigate. On the other hand, the open text responses indicate that the residents themselves are also very aware of both their own and the endogenous perceptions of Järva (and specific neighborhoods within the district). The external perceptions of Järva could as such also have been internalized within the locals to some degree – as self-stigma within residents and stigma by association within visitors ([Oittinen et al., 2024](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B63)), intertwining personal experiences with outsiders’ negative views.

Another contribution concerns the identification of typologies of place and meso- and micro-locations of fear for different place users. The integration of PPGIS-based mapping, spatial statistical analysis, and qualitative open-text responses enabled a triangulated approach to local place perceptions, largely confirming previous findings on typologies of safe and unsafe places ([Linhartová et al., 2022](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B52); [Ceccato & Snickars, 2000](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B11); [Guldåker et al., 2024](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B29)). Green areas, town squares, transit hubs, and commercial areas were repeatedly mentioned by both visitor and resident respondents, whereas the safety assessments of these locations were highly contextually dependent. Typically, visual appeal and social activity both enhanced safety perceptions, while poor maintenance, anti-social behavior and personal or second-hand crime experiences negatively affected them (aligning with previous research, e.g., [Gerber et al., 2010](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B28); [Lupton, 1999](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B57); [Guldåker et al., 2024](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B29)). The cluster analysis suggests that only a select few places account for a majority of perceived unsafe locations, similar to recent Swedish studies ([Guldåker et al., 2024](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B29); [Kronkvist, 2024](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B47)). From a broader perspective, unsafe and unavoidable locations differed between neighborhoods, place users, and temporal contexts. Locations within Tensta and Rinkeby were considered particularly unsafe but not unavoidable by residents, while Husby and Kista locations were reported as unsafe and unavoidable both day and night, especially by visitors. These differences may stem from the contrast between central Järva’s residential character and particularly Kista’s role as a commercial and transit hub. Residents of Rinkeby and Tensta may better navigate their neighborhoods at night, while Kista attracts diverse crowds who must pass through transit hubs and public spaces they perceive as unsafe. Open-text responses reinforce this fear, particularly around Kista’s bus transit hub, aligning with prior studies identifying transit nodes as crime attractors and sources of fear ([Brantingham & Brantingham, 1995](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B4); [Ceccato, 2013](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B9)). These findings suggest that perceptions of place typologies may vary based on place user positionalities, reinforcing the need for context-sensitive and user-informed approaches to urban safety interventions.

A third contribution relates to the intersection of fear research and territorial stigma. Not only do outsiders largely associate the Järva with crime, segregation, and socioeconomic challenges (greatly reflecting the district’s media representation), the findings also indicate that these narratives can reinforce “visual biases” related to the built environment. The disproportionate attribution of images depicting disorder and neglect to Järva likely reflects a self-reinforcing cycle of territorial stigma ([Wacquant, 2007](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B83)), as numerous studies find that signs of urban decay and disorder are associated with crime and poor safety ([Mellgren et al., 2011](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B58); [Ross & Jang, 2000](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B69); [Brunton‐smith & Sturgis, 2011](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B7)). [Wacquant (2007)](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B83) argues that territorial stigma, like ethnic stigma, can attribute presumed characteristics of a territory to its population, based solely on their residence. In Järva, where immigrant residents are often already problematized and several neighborhoods are officially designated ‘particularly vulnerable,’ such stigma risks legitimizing exclusionary urban policies that further marginalize communities. These concerns have already surfaced in public debate, where many view Järva as a de facto control zone, even before the introduction of temporary stop-and-search zones ([Moreno & Mattison, 2024](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B60)). Survey responses further reinforce these dynamics: consistent with previous research ([Permentier et al., 2009](https://www.scup.com/doi/10.18261/njc.27.1.7#core-collateral-B67)), place reputation emerged as a significant factor influencing reluctance to live in Järva. While safety concerns were frequently cited by non-residents, concerns about Järva’s remoteness, limited opportunity, and socioeconomic challenges were more common across all groups. The open-text responses suggest that perceptions of safety, crime, and structural disadvantage are closely intertwined, indicating that these perceptions may reinforce one another. As Wacquant notes, these overlapping perceptions not only shape how Järva is viewed by outsiders, but also contribute to its symbolic relegation and may, over time, exacerbate socioeconomic and spatial exclusion. Addressing these issues may therefore not only require crime prevention measures and improvements of the built environment, but also deliberate efforts to reshape public perceptions.

Finally, an additional methodological insight relates to operationalization of fear and safety. Notably, the lack of significance of many individual characteristics may partly stem from small sample sizes, but it may also suggest that in highly stigmatized areas like Järva, safety concerns may be shaped more by collective and spatial factors than personal vulnerabilities. The phrasing of the questions posed to respondents— “Is Järva a safe area?” and “What is your idea of safety in Järva?”— may have elicited responses anchored in public discourse rather than personal experience. Given the district’s stigmatization, both locals and outsiders may have aligned their assessments with dominant narratives. This is reinforced by the fact that outsiders’ perceptions of their own neighborhoods varied by gender and place of birth, suggesting that individual factors’ relationship with safety is more complex and context-dependent. The findings highlight both the value and difficulty of measuring perceptions of different types of place users, as the approach reveals underlying mechanisms of place perception while also highlighting the need for more carefully tailored survey instruments.

Conclusion and limitations
--------------------------

This study set out to assess the safety perceptions among locals and outsiders of the Stockholm district Järva. We examined in particular how these perceptions differ between the groups, the determining factors of the differences, the nature of assessed locations, and how the perceptions influence willingness to reside in Järva. The findings reveal significant perceptual differences based on familiarity and experiential knowledge, with outsiders viewing Järva as significantly less safe – although familiarity had a significant effect even within this group. While locals tended to view Järva as safe, this was dependent on the time of day, built environment conditions, and knowledge and experience of crime and antisocial activities. The mapping of (un)safe locations revealed strong spatial clustering of local fear and attachment, often tied to micro-scale typologies such as squares, malls, transport hubs, and green spaces. Finally, perceived safety significantly influenced willingness to reside in Järva, with outsiders and visitors more likely to reject the idea of living there due to safety concerns.

This study contributes to the intersection of environmental psychology, human geography, and crime and safety research by furthering our understanding of how varying relationships with places, including familiarity, attachment, and stigma, may affect our perceived safety. It also further showcases the relevancy of PPGIS-methodologies in safety research in capturing these complexities. Furthermore, the findings may inform policy and practice. The Kista transit hub, for instance, is a key concern for both residents and visitors, warranting targeted interventions that improve natural surveillance. Additionally, given the significant effect of increased experiential knowledge on safety, officials should prioritize campaigns, events, and initiatives that improve Järva’s image and strengthen local and inter-neighborhood connections. Ultimately, this may improve safety perceptions for both locals and outsiders, as well as social stability and connectivity within the city.

The study has several limitations that present opportunities for future research. The small sample of Järva visitors limited deeper analysis of how varying degrees of area interaction influence safety perceptions, due in part to difficulties reaching this group. Although surveys were distributed separately to locals and outsiders, both online and in person, open access via shared links meant a small risk of misclassification. While the survey was offered in both Swedish and English, language barriers may still have persisted given Järva’s large foreign-born population. The relatively young sample likely reflects both the comparably successful university-based recruitment and potential digital barriers tied to the PPGIS survey platform. Future studies could, if possible, use stratified sampling and engage in broader outreach through local organizations to improve demographic balance. The study also assumes differing levels of place attachment among residents, visitors, and outsiders, but this is not necessarily a given. One way forward would be to incorporate direct measures of attachment strength and further explore spatial variations in place attachment. This study also did not consider how proximity to Järva may shape outsider perceptions; examining potential distance decay or intensification effects could be valuable. Differences in safety question phrasing across groups may have influenced the results. While deemed necessary given the differing respondent positionalities in the current study, using uniform questions across all groups could help clarify whether observed patterns are robust. Self-selection bias is another concern, as Järva’s controversial reputation may have attracted respondents with strong opinions, potentially skewing results toward extreme views, whether negative perceptions or passionate and defensive residents. Lastly, the study’s cross-sectional design limits its ability to track evolving perceptions, especially as media narratives on gang violence have likely influenced recent views. Longitudinal studies with repeated surveys could provide insights into how safety perceptions and place attachment change over time.

Acknowledgements
----------------

We would like to thank the Stockholm Municipality, Järva city district administration, Citycon, Folkets Hus in Rinkeby and Husby, and numerous other local organizations and individuals for aiding us in distributing the survey. We would also like to thank Asta Hiippala at Mapita for guiding us in our design of the survey using the Maptionnaire platform. Finally, we thank the residents and non-residents of Järva for participating in the survey.

Perceptions of one’s neighborhood, such as feeling unsafe in one\`s neighborhood or lack of neighborhood cohesion, have been linked to poorer physical health (Robinette, Charles, & Gruenewald, 2016; Murayama, Fujiwara, & Kawachi, 2012; Robinette, Charles, Mogle, & Almeida, 2013). Objective aspects of neighborhoods, such as crime statistics and income, are also often assessed and associated with health (Weden, Carpiano, & Robert, 2008). However, here we focus on measures to assess subjective reports of neighborhood qualities, given evidence that neighborhood perceptions may show particularly strong links with health outcomes compared to objective assessments (Weden, Carpiano, & Robert, 2008).

​

Several aspects of neighborhood environment have been proposed as relevant for health outcomes. For example, lack of neighborhood social cohesion has been associated with self-rated physical health and physical symptoms (Murayama, Fujiwara, & Kawachi, 2012; Robinette, Charles, Mogle, & Almeida, 2013). However, reliable and valid measures have been scarce. The most frequently used measure, developed by Sampson, Raudenbush, and Earls (1997), consists of 5 items rated on a five-point scale (“people around here are willing to help their neighbors,” “this is a close-knit neighborhood,” “people in this neighborhood can be trusted,” “people in this neighborhood generally don’t get along with each other,” and “people in this neighborhood do not share the same values”). Variations of a subset of these items have also been used in some large-scale samples (e.g., the Midlife in the United States (MIDUS) study: “I could call on a neighbor for help if I needed it; People in my neighborhood trust each other”).

Another important feature of neighborhood environment is perceived neighborhood safety. Feeling unsafe in one’s neighborhood has been associated with later chronic health conditions (Robinette, Charles, & Gruenewald, 2016). No state-of-the art measures exist, but previously tested items assessed global perceptions of neighborhood safety, such as “…how safe do you feel walking alone in your neighborhood?”, which is rated by participants for both daytime and night-time (De Jesus, Puleo, Shelton, & Emmons, 2010). Slight variations have also been used in some large-scale studies. For example, the Midlife in the United States (MIDUS) study assessed participants\` ratings of “I feel safe being out alone in my neighborhood during the daytime” and “I feel safe being out alone in my neighborhood at night” (based on Keyes, 1998).

​

A closely related concept is perceived neighborhood disorder – the degree to which there is a lack of safety, peace, social control, and observance of the law in the neighborhood. Ross and Mirowsky (1999) developed the 15-item Neighborhood Disorder Scale, which assesses aspects of physical order/disorder (e.g., graffiti, vandalism, cleanliness) as well as social order/disorder (e.g., drug use in neighborhood, police protection), which includes perceptions of safety (e.g., “My neighborhood is safe”). Perceived neighborhood safety and neighborhood disorder have been associated with physiological risk factors such as flatter diurnal cortisol slopes (Do et al., 2011; Karb, Elliott, Dowd, & Morenoff, 2012) and telomere shortness, even after adjusting for demographic and socioeconomic characteristics (Park, Verhoeven, Cuijpers, Reynolds Iii, & Penninx, 2015).

​

Other self-reported neighborhood characteristics have also been examined. For example, Mujahid and colleagues (2007) have developed psychometrically and econometrically valid subscales for social cohesion (4 items) and safety (3 items), aspects of aesthetic quality (6 items), walking environment (10 items), availability of healthy foods (4 items), violence (4 items), and activities with neighbors (5 items), and similar scales have been developed for other countries, as well as for urban vs rural regions.

​

Author(s) and Reviewer(s):

Prepared by Stefanie Mayer, PhD. Reviewed by Ana Diex-Roux, MD, PHD, MPH, Mahasin Mujahid, PhD, MS, FAHA, Belinda Needham, PhD, MA and Barbara Laraia, PhD, MPH, RD. If you have any comments on these measures, email [Stefanie.Mayer@ucsf.edu](mailto:Stefanie.Mayer@ucsf.edu). Version date: February 2018

​

References:

De Jesus, M., Puleo, E., Shelton, R. C., & Emmons, K. M. (2010). Associations between perceived social environment and neighborhood safety: Health implications. Health & Place, 16(5), 1007-1013.

​

Do, D. P., Diez Roux, A. V., Hajat, A., Auchincloss, A. H., Merkin, S. S., Ranjit, N., … Seeman, T. (2011). Circadian rhythm of cortisol and neighborhood characteristics in a population-based sample: The Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis. Health & Place, 17(2), 625–632.

​

Karb, R. A., Elliott, M. R., Dowd, J. B., & Morenoff, J. D. (2012). Neighborhood-level stressors, social support, and diurnal patterns of cortisol: The Chicago Community Adult Health Study. Social Science & Medicine, 75(6), 1038–1047.

​

Keyes, C.L.M., 1998. Social well-being. Soc. Psychol. Q. 61, 121–137, retrieved from ([http://www.jstor.org/stable/2787065)](http://www.jstor.org/stable/2787065).

​

Mujahid, M. S., Diez Roux, A. V., Morenoff, J. D., & Raghunathan, T. (2007). Assessing the measurement properties of neighborhood scales: from psychometrics to ecometrics. American journal of epidemiology, 165(8), 858-867.

​

Murayama, H., Fujiwara, Y., Kawachi, I. (2012). Social capital and health: A review of prospective multilevel studies. J Epidemiol, 22(3), 179-187.

​

Park, M., Verhoeven, J. E., Cuijpers, P., Reynolds Iii, C. F., & Penninx, B. W. J. H. (2015). Where You Live May Make You Old: The Association between Perceived Poor Neighborhood Quality and Leukocyte Telomere Length. PloS One, 10(6), e0128460.

​

Robinette, J. W., Charles, S. T., Almeida, D. M., & Gruenewald, T. L. (2016). Neighborhood features and physiological risk: An examination of allostatic load. Health & Place, 41, 110-118.

​

Robinette, J. W., Charles, S. T., Mogle, J. A., & Almeida, D. M. (2013). Neighborhood cohesion and daily well-being: Results from a diary study. Social Science & Medicine, 96, 174-182.

​

Ross, C. E., & Mirowsky, J. (1999). Disorder and decay: The concept and measurement of perceived neighborhood disorder. Urban Affairs Review, 34(3), 412-432.

​

. Author manuscript; available in PMC: 2023 Sep 1.

_Published in final edited form as:_ J Expo Sci Environ Epidemiol. 2022 Oct 19;33(2):207–217. doi: [10.1038/s41370-022-00486-x](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41370-022-00486-x)

Abstract
--------

### Background:

The communities we live in are central to our health. Neighborhood disadvantage is associated with worse physical and mental health and even early mortality, while resident sense of safety and positive neighborhood sentiment has been repeatedly linked to better physical and mental health outcomes. Therefore, understanding where negative neighborhood sentiment and safety are salient concerns can help inform public health interventions and as a result, improve health outcomes. To date, fear of crime and neighborhood sentiment data or indices have largely been based on the administration of time consuming and costly standardized surveys.

### Objective:

The current study aims to develop a Neighborhood Sentiment and Safety Index (NSSI) at the census tract level, building on publicly available data repositories, including the US Census and ACS surveys, Data Axle, and ESRI repositories.

### Methods:

The NSSI was created using Principal Component Analysis. Mineigen and minimum loading values were 1 and 0.3, respectively. Throughout the step-wise PCA process, variables were excluded if their loading value was below 0.3 or if variables loaded into multiple components.

### Results:

The novel index was validated against standardized survey items from a longitudinal cohort study in the Northeastern United States characterizing experiences of 1) Neighborhood Characteristics with a Pearson correlation of −0.34 (_p_ < 0.001) and, 2) Neighborhood Behavior Impact with a Pearson correlation of −0.33 (_p_ < 0.001). It also accurately predicted the Share Care Community Well Being Index (Spearman correlation = 0.46) and the neighborhood deprivation index (NDI) (Spearman correlation = −0.75).

### Significance:

Our NSSI can serve as a predictor of neighborhood experience where data is either unavailable or too resource consuming to practically implement in planned studies.

INTRODUCTION
------------

The neighborhoods we live in are important to our health. Independent of individual or family-level characteristics, neighborhood disadvantage is associated with worse physical and mental health and early mortality[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R1)–[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R6). Neighborhood satisfaction is found to be lower in resource deprived areas and, in turn, emotional responses to neighborhood conditions are less positive in these areas[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R7). While mechanisms are not completely understood, disadvantaged neighborhood environments are posited to elicit negative affect and psychological stress effects that get biologically embedded[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R8), [9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R9). A recent study used virtual reality to simulate neighborhood environments and linked exposure to neighborhood disadvantage with greater negative emotion and enhanced stress reactivity in a controlled laboratory setting[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R10).

Given that the neighborhoods we live in are central to our health, understanding which qualities of neighborhood sentiment and safety are most salient can help inform public health interventions and as a result, improve health outcomes[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R11)–[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R14). Assessing availability of social services and other resource-related conditions is important to characterizing neighborhood context and consequent sentiment[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R10), [15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R15)–[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R17). Additionally, sense of safety has been identified as a central aspect of neighborhood disadvantage[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R18), [19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R19). For example, evidence suggests that even when objective conditions such as green space, public transportation, and local amenities are evenly distributed, residents who perceive lower overall safety report lower levels of neighborhood satisfaction[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R7). Our group and others[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R20)–[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R22) have linked perceived crime levels and/or fear of crime in one’s community with higher levels of stress[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R21), [23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R23), greater exposure to other toxins[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R24), decreased mental health and physical functioning[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R21),[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R23), decreased leisure and outdoor leisure activity[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R25), increased risk of cardiorespiratory disease[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R20), [26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R26), [27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R27), less physical activity[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R28), and adverse birth outcomes[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R29). Similarly, perceptions of heightened community safety and positive neighborhood sentiment have been repeatedly linked to better physical and mental health outcomes[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R1), [28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R28), [30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R30). These findings emphasize the importance and relevance of perceived safety to overall neighborhood sentiment and health.

However, sense of safety and neighborhood sentiment data are often either unavailable to the public or burdensome to collect in larger scale epidemiological studies. Traditionally, fear of crime and neighborhood sentiment data used for the creation of neighborhood disadvantage indices have been largely based on the administration of time consuming and costly standardized surveys[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R31). Moreover, existing approaches to develop indices reflecting overall neighborhood safety and/or sentiment have been limited by poor spatial resolution and lack of validation capability, which makes the weight and usefulness of the indices uncertain, as well as limiting their utility in guiding more targeted public health interventions[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R31), [32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R32).

The objective of the current study was to develop and validate a Neighborhood Sentiment and Safety Index (NSSI) at the census tract level. In an effort to capture the lived neighborhood experience, inputs included a rich set of variables selected from widely available data, with a focus on variables related to neighborhood sentiments, wellbeing, and sense of safety[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R23), [33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R33)–[49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R49). We then rigorously validated the NSSI using individual level survey data on neighborhood, wellbeing, crime and safety perceptions, the Neighborhood Deprivation Index (NDI), as well as against the previously established Share Care Index[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R31). The NDI provides a measure of neighborhood deprivation at the census tract level, with higher values corresponding to more severe deprivation[50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R50),[51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R51). The NDI empirically summarizes eight census variables representing five domains: income/poverty, education, employment, housing, and occupation[50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R50),[51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R51).The Share Care Index brings together more than 600 established individual and social health risk factors into a single measure to quantify well-being across people and places[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R31). The current index is based on responses from more than 3 million surveys and 600+ social determinants of health[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R31).

MATERIALS AND METHODS
---------------------

### Study Area

We created the NSSI for Massachusetts at the census tract level with a focus on the Boston metropolitan area. While this index can be created for any state, the region was selected based on availability of individual-level participant data from an extant cohort residing in the area that could be leveraged to validate the created NSSI as detailed below[52](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R52), [53](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R53). The NSSI was derived using data primarily from 2010 in order to most optimally align with the timeframe of the validation cohort dataset and to allow for the use of the 2010 decennial census as a primary data source[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#FN4). Massachusetts has 14 counties across 7,800 square miles[54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R54). Approximately two thirds of the state population lives in rural regions (61.7%) and one third in urban regions (37.1%)[54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R54). In 2010, the Massachusetts total population was approximately 6.5 million with a median age of 39 years[54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R54). Of adults 18 and older, 86.3% had a high school degree or higher[54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R54) and the median annual household income was $62,072[54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R54). See [Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#T1) for racial composition of Massachusetts.

### Data Sources

We derived the NSSI using three data sources: 1) Environmental Systems Research Institute’s (ESRI) Crime Indices, 2) Data Axle’s Historical Business Data, and 3) variables from the United States (U.S.) Census and American Community Survey (ACS) previously used to characterize neighborhood context related to neighborhood sentiment and safety, including resource-related conditions, fear of crime and wellbeing.

ESRI’s Crime Indices incorporate information from the AGS National CrimeRisk database, which is based on an extensive analysis of several years of crime incidents reported by most U.S. law enforcement jurisdictions[55](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R55). These data are available at multiple spatial resolutions down to the block group level[55](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R55). The Crime Indices database includes nine standardized indexes for a range of serious crimes against both persons and property: personal crime, murder, rape, robbery, assault, property crime, burglary, larceny, and motor vehicle theft[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#FN5). For the purpose of this study, we used crime data from 2016, which was the most temporally aligned crime data available.

Data Axle’s Historical Business Data ranges from 1997–2021 and contains annual, geo-coded records of U.S. businesses and other organizations[56](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R56). Records include company information such as location, industry description, annual revenues, number of employees, and year established[56](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R56). Information on community businesses is important to consider as research supports that greater access to services like mental health counseling, health care, hospitals and pharmacies in one’s neighborhood is linked to reduced crime and improved sentiment; however, these relationships remain understudied[39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R39). We identified relevant businesses through North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) code searches and calculated the number of each resource within each census tract. Other resource-related conditions such as the presence of large transportation hubs, including bus depots and rail stations, have also been significantly correlated with many types of crime and contribute negatively to overall neighborhood sentiment[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R38), [40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R40). Likewise, limited access to health food stores and an increased number of establishments selling alcohol have been previously linked to diminished well-being, food insecurity, and crime[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R35), [36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R36), [44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R44), [46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R46).

The U.S. Census and American Community Surveys (ACS) provides datasets for public use, with personally identifiable information removed to ensure confidentiality[57](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R57). The census is taken via mail-in citizen self-reporting, with enumerators serving to spot-check randomly selected neighborhoods and communities to ensure data reliability[57](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R57). The data collected by the census is unparalleled in reach – in 2010 72% of U.S. households returned mailed questionnaires[57](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R57). Measures of income, income inequality and employment such as median household income, per capita income, and the Gini index of income inequality were found to be related to crime and feelings of fear[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R34), [42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R42), [47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R47), [49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R49). Unemployment also tracks with crime and feelings of safety[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R41), [43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R43), as do measures of education and access to education. Specifically, communities with higher levels of educational attainment have been shown to experience lower crime rates[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R33), [45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R45), [48](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R48).

### Data Availability

All data included in the derivation of the NSSI exists within data repositories that are accessible without cost or with a subscription or purchase agreement. The data from validating source, ShareCare, is publically available on their website. The NDI provided by Children’s Environmental Health Initiative (CEHI) is available through a data request to their repository. The cohort validating data in this paper was collected as part of the PRogramming of Intergenerational Stress Mechanisms (PRISM) pregnancy cohort study at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai. Due to human subjects confidentiality, data are not publicly available; however, a limited dataset may be obtained from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.

### Index Derivation

We began constructing the NSSI using a detailed geospatial database (198 variables) at the census-tract level constructed from the three data repositories described above. We omitted variables that were redundant or that had more than 10% missing cases (n=100 variables). This resulted in a dataset of 98 variables, which we standardized using z-scores in order to minimize differences in scale. Next, we conducted five rounds of Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to create a unified and parsimonious index. PCA is a data-reduction method that is often used to reduce the dimensionality of large datasets without loss of information[58](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R58), [59](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R59). In the first round of PCA, individual variables load together into components. In subsequent rounds of PCA, the components further load together into a new set of further consolidated components. We calculated a weighted average of the components using the loading as weights. Then, in the next stage we performed PCA using these new weighted variables which represent each component. After five rounds of PCA the data dimensionality was reduced adequately for analyzation. PCA is defined as an orthogonal linear transformation that converts the data to a new coordinate system such that the greatest variance by some scalar projection of the data comes to lie on the first coordinate (called the first principal component), the second greatest variance on the second coordinate, and so on[58](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R58). Mathematically, the transformation is defined by a set of size _l_ of _p_\-dimensional vectors of weights or coefficients w(k)\= (w1,…,wp)(k) that map each row vector x(i) of X to a new vector of principal component scores t(i) = (t1,…,tl)(i) , given by tk(i) = x(i) \* w(k) for i = 1,…,n k= 1,…,_l_ in such a way that the individual variables t1,…,t_l_ of **t** considered over the data set successively inherit the maximum possible variance from **X**, with each coefficient vector **w** constrained to be a unit vector (where _l_ is often selected to be less than _p_ to reduce dimensionality)[58](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R58).

In order to maximize variance, the first weight vector **w**(1) thus has to satisfy

w(1)\=arg max‖w‖\=1{∑i(t1)(i)2}\=arg max‖w‖\=1{∑i(x(i)⋅w)2}

With **w**(1) found, the first principal component of a data vector **x**(_i_) can then be given as a score _t_1(_i_) = **x**(_i_) \* **w**(1) in the transformed co-ordinates, or as the corresponding vector in the original variables, {**x**(_i_) \* **w**(1)} **w**(1)[58](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R58).

The _k_\-th component can be found by subtracting the first _k_ − 1 principal components from **X**:

and then finding the weight vector which extracts the maximum variance from this new data matrix

w(k)\=argmax‖w‖\=1{‖X^kw‖2}\=arg max{w⊤X^k⊤X^kww⊤w}

Each round produced weighted components based on the variable loadings, which were then used as the components for the subsequent round of PCA. Mineigen value and minimum loadings values were 1 and 0.3, respectively[58](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R58). The mineigen value specifies the critical eigenvalue that a component must display if that component is to be retained. Throughout the step-wise PCA process, variables were excluded if their loading value was below 0.3 or if variables loaded into multiple components. At the end of this process, the census tract-level index was generated, which was based on 33 variables summarized in [Table 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#T2), making the dataset easier to explore, visualize, and analyze. The final index is comprised of variables that describe the community including: race, crime, education, income, population size, community and legal services ([Table 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#T2)). Higher NSSI scores indicate more positive feelings of neighborhood sentiment and safety.

### Index validation

To validate the NSSI, we used four separate measures that capture neighborhood sentiment and sense of safety. Notably, more than 80% of the general population of Massachusetts lives in the Greater Boston metropolitan region[54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R54). Thus, we leveraged an existing cohort study recruited from this catchment area with relevant available data. For the first two measures used in the validation step, we used questionnaire data from the PRogramming of Intergenerational Stress Mechanisms (PRISM) study, which has been previously described[53](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R53). Briefly, PRISM is a prospective pregnancy cohort of mother-child pairs that was designed to investigate the effects of perinatal stress and other environmental exposures on child development. The PRISM study recruited N=390 English- or Spanish-speaking women ≥18 years of age receiving prenatal care from the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC) and the East Boston Neighborhood Health Center (EBNHC) in Boston, Massachusetts at 21.4 ± 9.1 weeks gestation from March 2011 to December 2013. Recruitment sites were chosen given desired heterogeneity in sociodemographic and racial/ethnic characteristics at both the individual and community level. All cohort procedures were approved by the human studies committee at the Brigham & Women’s Hospital (BWH); BIDMC ceded review to BWH.

Written informed consent was obtained by an in-person interview in the participant’s primary language. A subset of participants (n=195) with complete covariate data collected between 2010 and 2013 were included in the analysis to validate the NSSI. We compared both groups (participants with full information vs. those with missing data), by spatially plotting their locations over the research area and found that those that were excluded were not spatially distributed significantly differently than our current sample with full information. Second, we compared the demographic characteristics (race, education, financial strain, etc) between the two groups, and found no meaningful differences (see [supplemental materials](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#SD1)). Characteristics of PRISM participants included in these analyses are summarized in [Table 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#T3). Included participants were located largely within the Greater Boston metropolitan area including 143 census tracts for which individual-level data were available ([Figure 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#F1)). Data collected from pregnant women at baseline included information on neighborhood and block conditions, social cohesion (e.g., the extent to which they participate or engage in civic/group participation or undertake acts of reciprocity), informal social control, and corresponding sentiment, making it a strong validation dataset for our index.

For each set of survey items, we created a unique validation measure using step-wise PCA as described above: 1) Neighborhood Characteristics and, 2) Neighborhood Behavior Impact. To create a census tract-level validation value for each measure, we took the median index values of all participants within each tract; higher values represent more negative sentiment about neighborhood and block conditions and increased need to change behavior in response to negative neighborhood conditions, respectively.

To further confirm the NSSI, we compared it to a third validation measure: the Share Care Community Well-Being Index[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R31). This index was created by and is maintained by a partnership between Sharecare, the digital health company and the Boston University School of Public Health. The Share Care Community Well-Being Index is a highly reputed and often cited index comprised of two inter-related indices: The Well-Being Index (WBI) and the Social Determinants of Health Index (SDOHi)[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R31). These two indices are combined, assigning equal weight to each, into a single score that represents self-reported individual health-related behaviors and perceptions incorporating the individual’s living environment[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R31). The county-level WBI characterizes every county in the U.S.[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R31). We specifically focused on the WBI community dimension, defined by Share Care as: “You like where you live, feeling safe and having pride in your community”[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R31), as this dimension contextually aligned best with our index. Higher WBI community dimension scores reflect a more positive sense of community. Share Care data is publicly available through their website down to the county level.

Lastly, we compared the NSSI to the NDI through the Children’s Environmental Health Initiative (CEHI)[50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R50),[51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R51). CEHI’s NDI empirically summarizes eight American Community Survey (ACS) variables representing five domains: income/poverty, education, employment, housing, and occupation[50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R50),[51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R51). The eight variables from the 2006–2010 American Community Survey include the percent of: (1) males in management and professional occupations; (2) crowded housing; (3) households in poverty; (4) female-headed households with dependents; (5) households on public assistance; (6) households with earnings less than $30,000 per year; (7) individuals with less than a high school education; and (8) individuals that are unemployed[50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R50),[51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R51). Similar to the NSSI, the NDI is calculated at the 2010 census tract level using a principal components analysis[50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R50),[51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R51). Higher NDI scores indicate greater disadvantage.

RESULTS
-------

After conducting five cycles of PCA, we generated the full index, which contained 33 variables, measuring race, crime, population size, education, income, and social services across 1271 census tracts (see [Table 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#T2) for the full list of items). The NSSI ranged from −0.88 to 3.78, with higher levels indicating more positive feelings of neighborhood sentiment and safety. [Figure 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#F2) presents a geospatial rendering of the index across all available census tracts, while [Figure 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#F3) is zoomed in to the Greater Boston metropolitan area. As can be seen in the [Figure 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#F3), in the center of Boston and near institutions of higher education, the NSSI is high, reflecting for example, access to resources and lower crime.

The Pearson correlation between the NSSI and the Neighborhood Characteristic validation measure derived using PRISM cohort data was −0.34 (_p_ < 0.001). Similarly, the Pearson correlation with the Neighborhood Behavior Impact validation item was −0.33 (_p_ < 0.001). These negative correlations indicate that higher levels of the NSSI represent positive sentiments about neighborhood and block conditions and higher feeling of safety, while as lower levels of Neighborhood Characteristics and Neighborhood Behavior Impact validations items indicate higher levels of positive sentiment.

Next, we validated the NSSI using The Share Care Well-Being Index. While The Share Care Well Being Index contains multiple dimensions including physical, social, financial, etc., we specifically focused on the community dimension, defined by Share Care as “You like where you live, feeling safe and having pride in your community”[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R31). Due to the Share Care Index being available publicly only at the county level, NSSI county rankings were calculated. NSSI county rankings were determined by taking the mean NSSI values for the tract excluding outliers. [Figure 4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#F4) compares the ranking by county using the Share Care Community Well-Being Dimension Index and the Neighborhood Sentiment and Safety Index. Because the Share Care Well-Being Index value differences between counties is small, the actual rank within the top and bottom halves are not meaningful[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R31). For example, the Share Care Community Well-Being Dimension values for Norfolk County, Barnstable County, and Middlesex County was 66 out of 100 with Dukes and Plymouth ranked 65. Therefore, we dichotomized the data at the 50th percentile and examined whether the counties predicted in the upper versus lower half using the Share Care Community Well-Being Index corresponded to the same counties predicted to be in the upper versus lower half by the NSSI. After removing Franklin and Berkshire counties, the NSSI accurately predicted four of the six counties ranked in the upper half and four of the six counties ranked in the lower half by the Share Care’s Community Dimension (Spearman correlation = 0.46)(see footnote [2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#FN5)). Specifically, the NSSI ranked Dukes, Barnstable, Middlesex, Norfolk and Plymouth counties in the top half of the rankings, as did the Share Care Community Well-Being Dimension[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R31). Similarly, NSSI recorded Worcester, Nantucket, Suffolk, Bristol and Hampshire in the bottom half of rankings, as did the Share Care Community Well-Being Dimension[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10010937/#R31). The two incongruent counties included Hampden, which the NSSI predicted to be in the top dimension (ranked 2nd) and Share Care predicted in the bottom (ranked 11th), and Essex, which the NSSI predicted to be ranked 7th and Share Care predicted to be ranked 6th.
