. Author manuscript; available in PMC: 2021 Aug 1.

_Published in final edited form as:_ J Interpers Violence. 2019 May 2;36(15-16):NP8615–NP8642. doi: [10.1177/0886260519844281](https://doi.org/10.1177/0886260519844281)

Abstract
--------

Community violence is a complex phenomenon and many theories have been put forth to explain the causes of community violence and disparities in community violence across neighborhoods. One notable theory, Collective Efficacy Theory (CET), posits that collective efficacy (i.e., a neighborhood’s social cohesion and informal social control) mediates the association between concentrated disadvantage and community violence. As CET theorizes an inverse feedback loop between collective efficacy and community violence, collective efficacy could mitigate the link between neighborhood disadvantage and community violence. The current study examines the reciprocal association between collective efficacy and community violence exposure using data from 604 low-resourced, urban African American 9th grade students from a large Midwestern city. Data were collected at 6-month intervals over 2 years. Significant cross-sectional associations were found between each of the collective efficacy constructs (social cohesion and informal social control) and community violence exposure, although no significant longitudinal cross-lagged associations were found. There were positive cross-sectional associations between (a) collective efficacy and community violence exposure and (b) informal social control and community violence exposure; however, the association between social cohesion and community violence exposure was negative. Associations between overall collective efficacy, as well as its subscales, and community violence exposure were consistent with hypothesized directions for social cohesion, but not for collective efficacy or informal social control. Findings support the use of collective efficacy as two constructs, rather than a single construct as proposed by [Sampson et al. (1997)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R42). Implications for expanding original assumptions of CET are discussed.

**Keywords:** Community violence exposure, collective efficacy, African American adolescents, cross-lagged panel model, informal social control, social cohesion

* * *

African American adolescents have disproportionately high rates of exposure to neighborhood and community violence. In the United States (U.S.), two-thirds of youth, ages 14-17, have been exposed to community violence during their lives, and half have been exposed to community violence in the past year ([Finkelhor, Turner, Ormrod, Hamby, & Kracke, 2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R18)). However, rates among African American adolescents are noticeably higher; for African American adolescents, estimates of lifetime community violence exposure range from 46-95% ([Gaylord-Harden, Cunningham, & Zelencik, 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R19); Self-Brown et al., 2006). African American adolescents are 6 to 9 times more likely to be victims of homicide than Caucasian adolescents ([Bureau of Justice Statistics \[BJS\], 2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R8)). In addition, compared to Caucasian and Latino individuals, African Americans are victims of serious violent crimes, like assault or robbery, at markedly higher rates ([BJS, 2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R9)).

Several factors likely impact differential levels of neighborhood and community violence. Collective efficacy, defined as a neighborhood or community’s social cohesion and willingness to enact informal social control on behaviors within the neighborhood/community boundaries ([Sampson, Raudenbush, & Earls, 1997](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R42)), is one well-researched theory to explain differences in community violence between neighborhoods ([Sampson, 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R41)). The extant research literature suggests that, over time, neighborhoods with higher levels of collective efficacy tend to have lower levels of community violence (e.g., [Ahern et al., 2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R1); [Sampson et al., 1997](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R42), [Sampson, 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R41)). Conversely, relatively little is known about the influence, over time, of community violence on a neighborhood’s collective efficacy. In light of the chronic community violence exposure many African American adolescents experience and the associated adverse sequelae of such exposure, it is imperative to better understand factors that potentially mitigate neighborhood and community violence, such as collective efficacy. The present study examines the reciprocal association between collective efficacy and community violence exposure in a sample of low-resourced (i.e., low-income, limited access to neighborhood resources), urban African American adolescents, to further explore the relevance of collective efficacy theory to community violence exposure and violence reduction.

Exposure to Community Violence
------------------------------

Exposure to community violence includes a range of experiences: (a) hearing about violence in one’s community, (b) witnessing violence in the community, and (c) direct violent victimization ([McDonald, Deatrick, Kassam-Adams, & Richmond, 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R31)). For the purposes of this study, community violence is defined as “deliberate acts intended to cause physical harm against a person or persons in the community” ([Cooley, Turner, & Beidel, 1995](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R14)), specifically acts perpetrated in one’s own neighborhood. Compared to other ethnic groups, low-resourced, urban African American adolescents are at highest risk for community violence exposure ([Aisenberg & Herrenkohl, 2008](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R2)), due to the cumulative violence exposure risk of their ethnicity (Zimmerman & Messner, 2013), neighborhood disadvantage ([Chamberlain & Hipp, 2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R12)), and urban neighborhood ([Truman & Morgan, 2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R48)). A study by Zimmerman and Messner (2013) compared the likelihood of community violence exposure among White and Black adolescents, and found that Black adolescents were 112% more likely to report community violence exposure. In another study, Richards and colleagues (2015) employed a daily sampling method to gauge urban, low-resourced African American adolescents’ exposure to community violence. In this study ([Richards et al., 2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R36)), while individual levels of violence exposure varied (e.g., some didn’t report exposure to violence every day, while others reported exposure to as many as 18 violent incidents on a single day), these youth experienced one violent incident per day, on average. Another study reported that 20-30% of African American youth were chronically exposed to high levels of community violence, while many other African American youth experienced chronic low levels of exposure ([Lambert, Nylund-Gibson, Copeland-Linder, & Ialongo, 2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R29)). These studies reveal that many African American adolescents are exposed to at least some community violence, and some are frequently exposed to such incidents.

Community violence exposure has been associated with emotional disturbances, such as anxiety ([Gaylord-Harden, Cunningham, & Zelencik, 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R19)), depression (Kennedy, Bybee, Sullivan, & Greeson, 2010), and suicidality ([Bennett & Joe, 2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R5)). Community violence exposure also has been linked to behavioral problems such as aggression and interpersonal violence ([Barroso et al., 2008](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R4)), substance use ([Voisin, Patel, Hong, Takahashi, & Gaylord-Harden, 2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R50)), and risky sexual behavior ([Voisin et al., 2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R50)). A better understanding of causes and ameliorators of community violence exposure is vital, considering the elevated risk for community violence exposure and the associated adverse outcomes for low-resourced, urban African American adolescents.

Collective Efficacy
-------------------

Neighborhoods experiencing higher levels of concentrated disadvantage (e.g., high percentage of families below poverty line and receiving public assistance, high levels of unemployment) often experience more community violence ([Sampson, 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R41)). Further, [Sampson et al. (1997)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R42), cross-sectionally studying 8,782 residents across 343 neighborhood clusters in Chicago, found that collective efficacy was negatively associated with neighborhood/community violence, and that the construct mediated the association between concentrated neighborhood disadvantage and community violence. Specifically, concentrated disadvantage was negatively associated with collective efficacy, and collective efficacy was negatively associated with community violence. Thus, collective efficacy may serve as a mechanism through which neighborhood disadvantage predicts community violence and, as such, may help explain the disparate levels of community violence between neighborhoods ([Sampson, 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R41)).

According to [Sampson (2012)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R41), Collective Efficacy Theory (CET) may explain and predict levels of neighborhood violent crime, as well as account for disproportionate levels of crime and community violence in demographically-similar neighborhoods. CET proposes that concentrated neighborhood disadvantage influences violent crime through collective efficacy; furthermore, concentrated disadvantage reduces collective efficacy ([Sampson, 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R41)). Decreases in collective efficacy lead to increases in violent crime ([Sampson, 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R41)). Additionally, CET posits a reciprocal and inverse relation between collective efficacy and community violence, such that lower collective efficacy leads to higher violence, and increases in violence reduce collective efficacy ([Sampson, 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R41)).

Collective efficacy is thought to affect community violence through the activation and utilization of social ties. While social cohesion within a neighborhood is important to achieving neighborhood goals, it is not sufficient; social networks and trust may facilitate social control, but it does not guarantee it ([Sampson, 2008](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R40)). For social networks to be functional in reducing community violence, these ties must be accompanied by a collective desire and capacity to regulate behavior ([Sampson et al., 1997](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R42)). Thus, collective efficacy, or the process of activating social ties to control crime ([Sampson, 2008](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R40)), requires both social cohesion and informal social control to be efficacious in reducing violent crime. Social ties within a neighborhood facilitate trust and support among members, while informal social control ensures that these social ties are activated to regulate violent behavior within the confines of the neighborhood.

Since the inception of CET, many studies have supported the main assertion of the theory: collective efficacy is related to violence. As noted earlier, [Sampson et al. (1997)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R42) predicted and demonstrated that higher collective efficacy was associated with both lower perceived and actual community violence; collective efficacy was negatively associated with perceived community violence, and a 2-standard deviation increase in collective efficacy was associated with a (a) 30% decrease in the likelihood of actual violent victimization, and (b) 40% decrease in expected homicide rates. [Sampson, Raudenbush, and Earls (1998)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R43) found that neighborhoods with higher collective efficacy had 40% lower violent crime rates than neighborhoods with lower collective efficacy; these findings have been replicated more recently by other researchers, in other metropolitan cities and neighborhoods across the globe, in addition to the early work examining Chicago neighborhoods. In New York, for example, the violent victimization rate for neighborhoods with low collective efficacy was double the rate of violent victimization for neighborhoods with high collective efficacy ([Ahern et al., 2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R1)). In London, [Sutherland, Brunton-Smith, and Jackson (2013)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R46) found a direct, negative association between collective efficacy and police-recorded violence. In Australia, [Mazerolle, Wickes, and McBroom (2010)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R30) found that higher levels of collective efficacy were associated with lower levels of violent victimization. Additionally, in Sweden, [Sampson and Wikström (2008)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R44) concluded that collective efficacy was directly and negatively associated with community violence.

Although many studies have supported the central assertion of CET (i.e., a direct, negative association between collective efficacy and community violence), other studies have found different results. [Hipp and Wickes (2017)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R23), examining roughly 6,000 adult residents in Brisbane, Australia over several years, were unable to find evidence for a direct link between collective efficacy and community violence longitudinally. Rather, they found an indirect association between collective efficacy and community violence through concentrated disadvantage, in which higher levels of collective efficacy reduced levels of concentrated disadvantage, and lower levels of concentrated disadvantage were associated with lower levels of violence. They also found a positive association between collective efficacy and community violence. This association was significant in 2-year lagged models, but not in 5-year lagged models. Other findings question the cohesiveness of the collective efficacy subscales. Using a sample of 800 adult residents in Arizona, [Armstrong, Katz, and Schnebly (2015)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R3) tested the cross-sectional association between collective efficacy and neighborhood violence, along with the association between the subscales of collective efficacy (i.e., social cohesion and informal social control) and neighborhood violence. In separate equations, when collective efficacy and its subscales were entered as predictors into regression models, with violent crime as the outcome variable, each measure of collective efficacy significantly predicted violent crime in the expected direction. However, when social cohesion and informal social control were included together in a regression model, only social cohesion predicted violent crime, suggesting that collective efficacy may not be adequately described by a single factor.

In contrast to the many research studies establishing the influence of collective efficacy on community violence, the reciprocal association between community violence and collective efficacy is relatively understudied ([Sampson, 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R41)), particularly so for African American adolescents. Although many of the longitudinal studies, wherein collective efficacy predicts community violence, control for prior violent crime ([Sampson, 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R41)), few studies directly test a reciprocal association between the two constructs. However, the reported studies that have tested for direct reciprocal effects found that violent crime has a negative influence on collective efficacy. Armstrong and colleagues (2015) reported a negative reciprocal relation between neighborhood violence and social cohesion. Duncan, Duncan, Okut, Stryker, and Hix-Small (2003) found that greater perceptions of neighborhood violent crime and more violent crime arrests were associated with less collective efficacy. Sampson and Raudenbush (1999) found a negative relation between robbery, a type of violent crime, and collective efficacy.

Reciprocity between collective efficacy and community violence presents a unique opportunity for preventive intervention, as well as cause for concern. In communities where collective efficacy is high or increasing, levels of community violence would be expected to decrease, thereby leading to further increases in collective efficacy. However, for communities with low or decreasing collective efficacy, expected subsequent increases in community violence and the potential of a negative feedback loop could exacerbate current problems.

The current study focuses on adolescents who experience substantial challenges associated with community violence and responds to the need for longitudinal examinations of reciprocal relations within CET ([Hipp & Wo, 2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R24); [Sampson, 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R41)) that might inform preventive interventions for these adolescents. Given the cumulative risk for community violence exposure among low-resourced, urban African American adolescents, as associated with ethnicity, socio-economic status, and neighborhood type, examining the collective efficacy and community violence exposure among these youth is of utmost importance. Anchored in CET, we hypothesized a bidirectional association between collective efficacy and its subscales and community violence exposure, such that youth reporting higher perceptions of collective efficacy would report lower levels of community violence exposure, and youth reporting more community violence exposure would report lower perceptions of collective efficacy. The present study addresses a critical research gap by examining the relation between collective efficacy and community violence exposure within a sample of low-resourced, urban African American adolescents.

Method
------

### Participants

This study used data collected as part of a larger study. The larger study was a randomized controlled efficacy trial of a culturally-adapted coping with stress prevention intervention for African American adolescents (for more information about the intervention, see: ([Robinson et al., 2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R37); [Robinson, Droege, Case, & Jason, 2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R38)). Data was collected from September 2014 to June 2017. Participants were recruited from the entire ninth grade classes at four predominantly African American (i.e., ≥ 85% African American student body) public high schools in a large Midwestern city. Approximately 75% of enrolled ninth grade students returned assent and parent/guardian permission to participate.

A total of 766 adolescents were recruited (i.e., both active parental consent and child assent), resulting in a 75% participation rate. This study utilized only African American participants’ data (n = 604). Slightly more than half of the participants for this study were female (54.6%) and the mean age of participants was 14.5 years (_SD_ = .58). Participating schools served mostly low-income students (> 85% of students at participating schools were low-income) and the majority of study participants were low resourced (i.e., low-income, limited access to neighborhood resources). Approximately 77% of participants lived in households that received food stamps. When surveyed about access to and use of neighborhood resources such as access to medical services or public transportation, only 3% of participants reported access to all neighborhood resources (see [Measures section](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#S6) below for more details).This study was approved by DePaul University’s Institutional Review Board and the public school district’s research review board.

### Procedure

Two cohorts of participants were recruited during their ninth grade year, in 2014 and 2015and each cohort was followed through the end of their 10th grade year. Recruitment occurred at school registration events, in homeroom classes, and during lunch. After obtaining parent/guardian permission and adolescent assent to participate, the adolescents completed a screening assessment to determine current suicide risk. Students at imminent risk for suicide (i.e., scored above a given threshold on a self-report suicide screening assessment or endorsed critical items related to suicide) were referred to the on-site school-based health center (SBHC) for a comprehensive assessment of their suicide risk status. Those participants not at imminent risk were eligible for participation and were randomized into the intervention or standard care control condition (n = 542). Of the 604 consented and assented students, 62 participants were not randomized due to imminent identified suicide risk or due to incomplete assessments. Randomized participants were assessed four times: (1) baseline, (2) post-intervention, (3) 6 months after completion of the intervention, and (4) 12 months after completion of the intervention. Student participants received a modest compensation for completing each assessment; $7 for completing the screener and $15 for completing each of the four waves of assessments.

### Measures

#### Demographic characteristics.

Demographic characteristics were obtained using 17 items assessing variables such as age, sex, ethnicity, religious involvement, family size/constellation, highest level of parental education, parent employment, and household income sources. For this study, age and sex were included in the analyses. Age has been associated with elevated levels of collective efficacy within neighborhoods ([Sampson et al., 1997](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R42)) and with increases in exposure to community violence during adolescence ([Finkelhor et al., 2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R18)). Sex also has been associated with violence exposure, with males reporting more violence exposure than females ([Chen, 2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R13)). While sex has not generally been associated with differences in collective efficacy ([Armstrong et al., 2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R3); [Sampson et al., 1997](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R42)), it is frequently included as a covariate to account for potential effects ([Armstrong et al., 2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R3); [Duncan et al., 2003](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R15)). In this study, age and sex were included as covariates.

#### Neighborhood resources.

The Chicago Youth Development Study Neighborhood scale (CYDS; [Tolan, Gorman-Smith, & Henry, 2001](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R47)) was used to measure participants’ access to resources within their neighborhood. The CYDS Neighborhood scale consists of 47 items, with six subscales: (a) sense of belonging, (b) social support, (c) perceived community problems, (d) community involvement, (e) community resources available, and (f) fear of crime. For this study, the community resources available subscale was used to determine access to neighborhood resources. This subscale consists of 13 true-false items, nine of which were scored to determine youth access to resources (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention \[CDC\], 2005; [Tolan et al., 2001](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R47)). Sample items included “there is a clinic or other medical services near my neighborhood,” “there are parks that we can use in or near my neighborhood,” and “public transportation is convenient for me to use.” The community resources available subscale of the CYDS Neighborhood scale had a Cronbach’s alpha of .61 in this sample.

#### American Community Survey.

Two neighborhood-level covariates were included in the models: (a) education (i.e., percentage of adult residents within a census tract with a least a Bachelor’s degree) and (b) population density (i.e., the number of occupied housing units in a census tract per 1,000 people). Participant addresses were geocoded to determine residential census tract, and the 2012-2016 American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates of population density and education level were used (U.S. Census Bureau, 2017a; U.S. Census Bureau, 2017b). The ACS, conducted yearly, is a nationwide survey of information such as age, race, income, home value, education level, and housing occupancy; a representative sample consisting of approximately three million people served to create estimates of variables at the tract, city, county, state, and country level.

#### Community violence exposure.

Community violence exposure was assessed by the Children’s Report of Exposure to Violence (CREV; [Cooley, Turner, & Beidel, 1995](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R14)). The CREV measures community violence exposure over the past year, utilizing a 29-item and 5-point Likert-type scale (i.e., 0 = no, never to 4 = every day). The measure assesses four factors of violence exposure: (a) media, (b) reports by other people, (c) direct exposure, and (d) direct experience. For this study, only the reports by other people, direct witnessing, and direct experience questions were used. Total scores for these items ranged from zero to 100, with higher scores indicating more exposure to violence. The CREV has demonstrated good construct validity, test-retest reliability (_r_ = .75) and internal consistency (α = .78), in a predominantly African American sample consisting of children and adolescents ([Cooley et al., 1995](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R14)). In this study, the Cronbach’s alpha for the CREV was .93.

#### Collective Efficacy.

To measure collective efficacy, two 5-item scales were used: (a) informal social control and (b) social cohesion ([Sampson et al., 1997](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R42)). Informal social control was measured using a 4-point Likert-type scale (i.e., 4 = very likely to 1 = very unlikely). Participants were asked how likely it was that neighborhood members would intervene in a given situation. An example question included: “If a child was showing disrespect to an adult, how likely is it that your neighbors would do something about it?” Social cohesion was measured using a 4-point Likert-type scale (i.e., 4 = strongly agree to 1 = strongly disagree). An example question included “this is a close-knit neighborhood.” Participants were asked to respond how much they agreed with each item.

In a previous study, social cohesion and informal social control were highly correlated (_r_ = .80; [Sampson et al., 1997](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R42)). Similarly, in this study, social cohesion and informal social control were significantly correlated (see [Table 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#T2)); so, following the recommendation of [Sampson et al. (1997)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R42), scores were averaged to create a collective efficacy score; higher scores indicated higher levels of collective efficacy. This strategy has been frequently used to study collective efficacy ([Duncan, Duncan, Okut, Strycker, & Hix-Small, 2003](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R15); [Odgers et al., 2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R33)). [Sampson et al. (1997)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R42) found evidence of construct validity, and acceptable internal consistency (α=.79), when scores were averaged. In this study, the Cronbach’s alpha for the full 10-item measure was .73. The Cronbach’s alphas for the social cohesion and informal social control subscales were .41 and .77, respectively. For this study, either mean collective efficacy or one of the subscale scores were used in each model.

### Analytic Strategy

This study used a cross-lagged panel analysis to examine reciprocal associations between collective efficacy, or one of its subscales, and community violence exposure, over time. The cross-lagged panel model (CLPM) is a type of path model used to examine the influence of two or more variables on each other over time ([Hamaker, Kuiper, & Grasman, 2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R21)). The longitudinal, cross-lagged design of CLPM allows for testing reciprocal effects, the determination of causally dominant variables, and the examination of temporal construct stability ([Hamaker et al., 2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R21)). CLPM was used to test the hypotheses that inverse bidirectional relations would exist between collective efficacy, or one of its subscales, and community violence exposure. All hypotheses were tested using CLPM and all four waves of data. Data was analyzed using Mplus version 8 ([Muthen & Muthen, 1998-2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R32)). Several indices were examined to determine model fit (i.e., chi-square, root mean square error of approximation \[RMSEA\], comparative fit index \[CFI\], standardized root mean square residual \[SRMR\], following recommendations by [Kline (2016)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R27).

To evaluate the reported fit statistics for each model, several indicators were used. First, for the chi-square test, a non-significant (i.e., p > .05) would indicate a good fit. However, the chi-square model fit test is sensitive to sample size ([Bentler & Bonett, 1980](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R6)), and given the sample size reported, significant models may not indicate bad-fitting models. Thus, other indicators will be assessed in conjunction with the chi-square statistic. For the RMSEA and SRMR fit statistics, coefficients closer to zero indicate better fitting models ([Kline, 2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R27)); generally, a coefficient less than .05 on would indicate excellent fit, while a coefficient below .08 would indicate acceptable fit ([Browne & Cudeck, 1993](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R7)). For CFI, values closer to 1 indicate better fit, and recommendations for cut-offs include .95 and .90 for good and acceptable fit, respectively ([Byrne, 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R10); [Hu and Bentler, 1999](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R25)). However, it should be noted that these cutoffs are often arbitrary ([Lai & Green, 2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R28)), and an examination of model fit should include a holistic view of multiple indices, in conjunction with theory.

Multiple models were estimated for each model containing either collective efficacy or one of its subscales, and community violence exposure. To determine covariate significance, reduced models were estimated, with two waves of data. Covariates included age, gender (coded as 0 = male, 1 = female), education, population density, and intervention condition (coded as 0 = control condition, 1 = intervention condition). Significant covariates were included in full, 4-wave models. Using four waves of data, six full models were estimated for each collective efficacy variable (i.e., collective efficacy, social cohesion, informal social control), beginning with a model with all free parameters, and fixing parameters to equality across time in successive models, until a model with all fixed parameters was estimated. Models were estimated fixing parameters in the following order: (a) Model 1- all parameters freely estimated, (b) Model 2- autoregressive community violence exposure parameter fixed to equality over time, (c) Model 3- all autoregressive paths fixed to equality over time, (d) Model 4- all autoregressive paths and community violence exposure to collective efficacy (or subscale) fixed to equality over time, Model 5 - all autoregressive and cross-lagged paths fixed to equality over time, and (e) Model 6- all parameters fixed to equality over time. Full models were compared, and the model with the lowest Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) score was interpreted. Full Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML) estimation was used to account for missing data and utilize all available data, as FIML has been shown to provide unbiased estimates in a more efficient manner than other missing data methods ([Enders & Bandalos, 2001](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R17)). Bootstrapped models were estimated, using 5000 samples.

Results
-------

Data were examined to determine normal distribution. Items were examined using a plotted histogram, Q-Q plot, and skewness and kurtosis values. Variables were generally normally distributed, with skewness and kurtosis values between ±1.75. To protect against potential issues of non-normality and other potential violations of assumptions, bootstrapping was employed to calculate standard errors and confidence intervals.

Means and standard deviations of continuous covariates and main study variables are included in [Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#T1). Comparing Wave 1 and Wave 4 collective efficacy and community violence exposure scores, collective efficacy scores were relatively consistent across time, with a slight, statistically significant decrease in collective efficacy over time (5.2%; _F_(3,996) = 18.12, _p_ < .001). Social cohesion evidenced a slight, non-significant decrease over time (1.2%; _F_(3,996) = 2.320, _p_ = .074), while informal social control evidenced a larger, statistically significant decrease (8.8%; _F_(3,993) = 22.42, _p_ < .001). Community violence exposure showed a slightly larger decrease over time (22.2%), and this decrease was statistically significant, _F_(3,996) = 7.36, _p_ < .001.

### Reciprocal Effects of Collective Efficacy and Community Violence Exposure

A correlation matrix with continuous study variables may be found in [Table 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#T2). A reduced model, using Waves 1 and 2, was fit to test for significant covariates. Covariates included age, gender, intervention condition, population density, and education. Three covariates were significant. Age significantly predicted community violence exposure at Wave 1 (_b_ = 4.69, _SE_ = 1.24, _p_ < .001; β = .17, _SE_ = .05, _p_ < .001, 95% CI \[.083, .262\]), and intervention condition significantly predicted community violence exposure at Wave 2 (_b_ = 3.44, _SE_ = 1.60, _p_ = .032; β = .18, _SE_ = .09, _p_ = .034, 95% CI \[.013, .346\]). Education significantly predicted collective efficacy at Wave 1 (_b_ = −.04, _SE_ = .02. _p_ = .01; β = −.13, _SE_ = .05, _p_ = .008, 95% CI \[−.222, −.034\]). These three covariates were included in the full models.

The full models were estimated, including the significant covariates, and AIC values were compared to determine the best-fitting model. The model with all autoregressive and cross-lagged paths fixed to equality over time (i.e., Model 5) had the lowest AIC, and was interpreted. Model fit statistics were adequate (see [Table 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#T3)). See [Figure 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#F1) for standardized parameter estimates. Significant autoregressive effects existed across all waves for both collective efficacy and community violence exposure. No significant cross-lagged associations existed. Two within-wave associations existed between collective efficacy and community violence exposure, with positive associations at Wave 2 (_p_ = .038, 95% CI \[.004, .189\]) and Wave 3 (_p_ = .032, 95% CI \[.010, .215\]).

### Reciprocal Effects of Social Cohesion and Community Violence Exposure

In the reduced model testing the reciprocal association of social cohesion and community violence exposure, using Waves 1 and 2, three covariates were significant. Age significantly predicted community violence exposure at Wave 1 (_b_ = 4.69, _SE_ = 1.22, _p_ < .001; β = .17, _SE_ = .04, _p_ < .001, 95% CI \[.089, .262\]), and intervention condition significantly predicted community violence exposure at Wave 2 (_b_ = 3.53, _SE_ = 1.60, _p_ = .027; β = .19, _SE_ = .09, _p_ = .028, 95% CI \[.019, .351\]). Education level significantly predicted social cohesion at Wave 1 (_b_ = −.04, _SE_ = .02, _p_ = .015; β = −.12, _SE_ = .05, _p_ = .013, 95% CI \[−.215, − .025\]).

Full models were estimated, including significant covariates, and the model with the lowest AIC fixed the autoregressive community violence exposure paths to equality over time (i.e., Model 2). Model fit statistics were adequate (see [Table 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#T3)). See [Figure 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#F1) for standardized parameter estimates. Significant autoregressive effects were present across all waves for social cohesion and community violence exposure, but no significant cross-lagged effects were present. The within-wave association between Wave 1 social cohesion and community violence exposure was negative and significant _p_ < .001, 95% CI \[−.264, −.095\]).

### Reciprocal Effects of Informal Social Control and Community Violence Exposure

In the reduced model testing the reciprocal association of informal social control and community violence exposure, using Waves 1 and 2, four covariates were significant. Age was significantly associated with community violence exposure at Wave 1 (_b_ = 4.69, _SE_ = 1.24, _p_ < .001; β = .17, _SE_ = .05, _p_ < .001), and intervention condition was significantly associated with community violence exposure at Wave 2 (_b_ = 3.38, _SE_ = 1.61, _p =_ .035; β = .18, _SE_ = .09, _p_ = .037). Two variables were significantly associated with informal social control at Wave 1: gender (_b_ = .13, _SE_ = .06, _p_ = .041; β = .18, _SE_ = .09, _p =_ .040) and education (_b_ = −.04, _SE_ = .02, _p_ = .048; β = −.06, _SE_ = .03, _p_ = .048).

Full models, including significant covariates, were estimated. The model fixing all paths to equality over time (i.e., Model 6) had the lowest AIC. Model fit was adequate (see [Table 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#T3)). See [Figure 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#F1) for standardized parameter estimates. Significant autoregressive effects for both variables were present across all waves, but no significant cross-lagged associations existed. Within-wave associations between informal social control and community violence exposure were positive and significant across waves (_p_ < .001, 95% CI \[.047, .152\]).

Discussion
----------

This study expands existing theoretical assumptions relative to intensifiers and attenuators of youth violence, particularly for vulnerable and understudied adolescents. Within a sample of low-resourced, urban African American adolescents, the reciprocal relation between community violence exposure and collective efficacy, as well as the relation between community violence and the subscales of collective efficacy (i.e., social cohesion and informal social control) were examined, using four waves of data and spanning a 2-year period. As hypothesized, there were significant cross-sectional associations between the constructs of interest, after controlling for significant covariates (i.e., age, gender, population density, education). However, no significant cross-lagged associations were observed.

Our hypotheses were anchored in CET and the findings both supported and contradicted CET. Within our sample, a relation was found between collective efficacy and community violence, in accord with CET; however, the relation was positive, suggesting that adolescents reporting higher perceived collective efficacy were exposed to more community violence and this aspect of our finding contradicts CET. When we examined the subscales of collective efficacy, an inverse relation was found between social cohesion and community violence exposure, suggesting that adolescents reporting higher perceived neighborhood social cohesion were exposed to less community violence and this is consistent with original conceptualizations of CET. In contrast, a positive relation was found between informal social control and community violence, suggesting that adolescents reporting higher perceived neighborhood informal social control were exposed to more community violence and this contradicts original conceptualizations of CET. In sum, both total scale and subscale indices of collective efficacy evidenced support and non-support of traditional CET, within our sample of low-resourced, urban African American adolescents.

Our findings, supporting the assertions of earlier work (e.g., [Armstrong et al., 2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R3); [Hipp & Wickes, 2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R23)), highlight aspects of CET, which warrant additional consideration. Our significant findings are cross-sectional; thus, it is impossible to determine temporal ordering of effects. Regardless, the findings support that some aspect(s) of collective efficacy are associated with lower levels of community violence exposure, among low-resourced urban African American adolescents. Furthermore, as with this study, the findings of other studies have been mixed. For example, [Hipp and Wickes (2017)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R23) reported a positive association between collective efficacy and community violence. This positive association was significant in 2-year longitudinal models, but not in 5-year longitudinal models. Additionally, the differential effects among collective efficacy subscales highlight concerns about the dimensionality of collective efficacy. [Armstrong et al. (2015)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R3) found that, when including both social cohesion and willingness to intervene in a model, only social cohesion significantly predicted neighborhood violence, and this relation was negative. These and other findings (e.g., [Rhineberger-Dunn & Carlson, 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R35); [Zhang, Messner, Liu, & Zhuo, 2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R51)) suggest that the construct of collective efficacy may not be unidimensional; as such, the reciprocal influence between collective efficacy and community violence may not always be negative.

The contrasting findings for the relation between informal social control/social cohesion and community violence exposure highlight potentially unique community responses to community violence and violence exposure. The negative relation between social cohesion and community violence exposure has been supported by theory and empirical studies ([Armstrong et al., 2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R3); [Sampson, 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R41)). Community violence is often associated with a decrease in feelings of cohesion and trust within a neighborhood. However, the positive association between informal social control and community violence exposure needs further examination. Although [Hipp and Wickes (2017)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R23) found significant positive associations in several of their lagged models of collective efficacy and violence, the authors did not examine the subscales of collective efficacy specifically, and they did not directly address the reasons for or implications of these findings.

Several potential explanations for these findings may exist. Lower levels of social cohesion may be associated with higher levels of community violence exposure, as individuals have less opportunity to interact with others in meaningful ways and enact informal social control ([Sampson, 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R41)). The negative association here is consistent with CET. However, higher levels of community violence exposure may prompt individuals or communities to enact more informal social control; crime itself may prompt neighborhood actions to reduce crime ([Durkheim, 1947](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R16)). Thus, the presence of crime in a community may act as a stimulus for neighborhood informal social control. However, this interpretation suggests a potential directional influence of violence on informal social control. Given the cross-sectional nature of the findings, and the lack of significant cross-lagged associations within a 6-month interval, it is difficult to determine whether such a relation exists. Examinations of the associations between social cohesion and informal social control, and between these variables and community violence using multiple temporal lags, may help to further explicate these potential relations.

Changing communities and technologies may affect neighborhood responses to violence and [Sampson and colleague’s (1997)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R42) original conceptualization of CET. [Sampson (2012)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R41) and others ([Armstrong et al., 2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R3); [Duncan et al., 2003](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R15)) have reported the negative influences of violence on collective efficacy. As originally proposed by [Sampson et al. (1997)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R42), community violence should decrease the trust and cohesion neighborhood residents have and decrease residents’ willingness to intervene ([Sampson, 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R41)). The decrease in trust and cohesion in response to violence highlight private-minded reactions to community violence (e.g., fear, helplessness, avoidance; [Schneider & Scheider, 1977](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R45)). However, other potential responses to community violence and crime exist. [Schneider and Schneider (1977)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R45) characterized these alternative responses as public-minded or empowering responses (e.g., protective neighboring, bystander intervention, social cohesion). Similarly, [Durkheim (1947)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R16) suggested that crime itself might empower citizens to engage in collective action to thwart violations of norms. Thus, it may be that, in response to community violence, some residents withdraw and reduce contact with neighborhood residents, while others are empowered to act to prevent future violence.

Several national incidents, occurring during this study’s data collection and analysis, have had high visibility and this visibility may have promulgated this public-minded response to violence. For example, a number of violent incidents incited protests in neighborhoods across the country and these protests received considerable media coverage. In the age of social media and with the attention that many of these protests receive, it is possible that responses to community violence will become more public-minded. Social media may serve as a medium to choreograph collective action and unite large groups of people around a common identity ([Gerbaudo, 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R20)). Social media and technological advances associated with cell phones and other devices enhance one’s ability to document actions, disseminate information, and gather individuals to act. These advancements in social media and technology may influence the expected negative relation between collective efficacy and community violence, as more people become aware of public-minded responses to local, national, and international events.

### Implications for Theory Expansion

The association between collective efficacy and community violence has been theorized and well documented ([Ahern et al., 2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R1); [Sampson, 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R41); [Sampson, 1997](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R42)). However, the reciprocal nature of collective efficacy and community violence is less established, especially in African American populations and with adolescent reports of collective efficacy perceptions. The present study addresses this research gap and has important implications to expand original assumptions of CET.

The findings of this study indicate two potential theoretical expansions regarding CET. First, the unidimensional construct of collective efficacy may need revisiting. For low-resourced, urban African American adolescents, social cohesion and informal social control may not coalesce into a single coherent construct; in other words, the constructs underlying collective efficacy may not coalesce into a unidimensional construct. Examining these constructs as a single factor may mask potentially different two-factor findings, particularly so for low-resourced African American adolescents who have chronic exposure to community violence. Several studies have examined the factor structure of collective efficacy and have proposed a two-factor solution, as opposed to a single factor ([Armstrong et al., 2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R3); [Hipp, 2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R22)). Second, for this population, the association between the subscales of collective efficacy and community violence exposure may not always be negative. Individuals may respond to community violence in private-minded and public-minded ways; social media and technological advances that facilitate the documenting and sharing of violent incidents, and action in response to violent incidents, may bolster public-minded responses.

### Implications for Prevention and Intervention

The findings of this and other studies have potential implications for youth preventive interventions, specifically by addressing the subscales of collective efficacy. The negative association between social cohesion and community violence exposure suggests that lower perceptions of social cohesion within a neighborhood are related to higher levels of community violence exposure. When exposed to community violence, the availability or perceived availability of social support for youth may decrease. Preventive interventions may intervene to help youth identify effective social supports within their neighborhoods, to potentially reduce community violence exposure or to reduce the likelihood of developing other behavioral or emotional outcomes associated with exposure. Alternatively, preventive interventions may benefit from a more multilevel perspective; interventions that help youth effectively identify issues affecting neighborhood social cohesion and support them in addressing these issues may build youth resilience while strengthening communities.

Before examining potential preventive interventions to address informal social control, more work is needed to understand the direction of influence between informal social control and community violence exposure. Caution should be taken when interpreting these cross-sectional findings; while informal social control and community violence are related, it is unclear whether they directly affect one another. Preventive interventions with youth have the potential for positive benefits, but also the potential for significant iatrogenic effects ([Rhule, 2005](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R39)). Understanding the factors that influence these variables, and the unique relation between informal social control and community violence exposure is necessary to protect against iatrogenic effects.

There are a several interventions addressing these variables or related constructs which may serve as models for effective preventive interventions. One such intervention, detailed by [Ohmer (2016)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R34), sought to increase collective efficacy, specifically social cohesion and informal social control, within a neighborhood by intervening with youth and adults. In the intervention, the community was engaged, youth and adults increased in social cohesion and willingness to intervene, and a community-based project was developed to address relevant community issues. A second relevant intervention is the Youth Empowerment Solutions (YES) program ([Zimmerman, Stewart, Morrel-Samuels, Franzen, & Reischl, 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R52)). This intervention incorporates empowerment theory to strengthen youth and prevent violence. The YES program works to increase social cohesion and reduce neighborhood violence by intervening with youth and adults, mentoring and monitoring youth, promoting nonviolence social norms and community involvement, and helping youth build and strengthen their community ([Zimmerman et al., 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7676433/#R52))

### Limitations and Future Research

The findings of the present study should be interpreted in light of limitations. First, collective efficacy and community violence exposure variables were assessed using self-report measures. While both measures have established psychometric properties, the use of self-report measures may introduce measurement errors, due to (a) socially desirable responding or (b) inability to accurately recall information, as in the case of the community violence exposure measure. Second, the generalizability of these findings may be limited, given the use of a single ethnicity and single geography population. Only urban African American adolescents from one Midwestern city were used in this study. Findings with more diverse samples and multiple locations may provide converging or diverging results. Third, the study lacked the proper sample size to estimate collective efficacy as a neighborhood-level construct. Sampson et al.’s (1997) original study aggregated the collective efficacy perceptions of multiple individuals per community area. Our sample size did not allow for such aggregation. The use of collective efficacy as an individual-level construct is subject to issues of bias and measurement error, whereas an aggregate variable would be able to account for some of this error and bias by incorporating multiple ratings.

Fourth, this study utilized adolescent perceptions of collective efficacy, rather than adult perceptions. Relatively few studies have examined adolescent perceptions of collective efficacy. As such, adolescents may view their communities differently than adults. In this study, age was included as a covariate; however, in the full models tested, age was not significantly associated with collective efficacy or either of its subscales. Lastly, data for this study was taken from a larger efficacy trial of a coping with stress preventive intervention. Participation in the intervention was not significantly related to any of the collective efficacy constructs, but was related to differences in community violence exposure at Wave 2. While participation in the intervention was included as a covariate in all analyses, it is possible that examining data collected from an efficacy trial may have influenced the outcomes in other unforeseen ways.

Future research directions emerge from this study to further examine the reciprocal association between collective efficacy and community violence. Multi-wave, longitudinal studies with larger sample sizes may expand on the collective efficacy-community violence link. A larger sample size may enable the exploration of these relations using collective efficacy as a neighborhood-level aggregate variable. In addition, it may be useful to examine the reciprocal associations between neighborhood-level social cohesion and community violence, and neighborhood-level informal social control and community violence. These studies would enable the examination of differential effects between the two constructs. Lastly, in-depth examinations of the predictors of responses to community violence would be useful. Understanding why and in what situations individuals react to community violence in public-minded or private-minded ways would allow for specific targeting in community-focused interventions.

### Conclusions

Researchers should consider multiple theoretical paths when examining collective efficacy and community violence. The present study indicates a need to re-examine both the structure of collective efficacy, as a construct, and the theorized directions of influence between collective efficacy and community violence, particularly so for vulnerable adolescent populations. We found that social cohesion and informal social control were differentially associated with community violence exposure. The potential for public-minded responses to community violence, even in communities plagued with chronic violent crime, suggests a consideration of these potential influences within CET.

While studies have identified a negative influence of violent crime on collective efficacy, some individuals and communities may respond to community violence by becoming more, rather than less, involved in community action. The direction of the influence of community violence may be contingent on multiple factors, including prior history with collective action and community violence; past or current cultural or contextual factors; the presence of action-oriented individuals; local, national, or international events; or any other number of psychological, sociological, or ecological factors. In sum, there is evidence that the original tenants of CET should be expanded; current investigations of CET should consider the potential public-minded responses that may occur and influence collective efficacy in light of violent events.

Sept 20 -- The Bureau of Justice Statistics, Office of Justice Programs, Department of Justice (DOJ) invites public comments to OMB by October 23, 2021 regarding the extension of the National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS) through 2024 and to ask all respondents age 16 or older about sexual orientation and gender identity beginning in January 2022.

The BJS National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS) is the nation's primary source of information on criminal victimization and is administered to persons 12 years or older living in sampled households located throughout the United States. Policy relevant subjects covered by the NCVS include intimate partner violence, hate crime, workplace violence, injury from victimization, guns and crime, the cost of crime, reporting to police, and crime against vulnerable populations, such as the elderly, juveniles, and persons with disabilities.  The NCVS is also a vehicle for the implementation of routine survey supplements that provide detailed information on timely and relevant topics such as identity theft, school crime, and contacts between the police and the public.

Each year, data are obtained from a nationally representative sample of about 240,000 interviews on criminal victimization, involving 160,000 unique persons in about 95,000 households. The estimated annual number of respondents is 124,663. The core NCVS includes the administration of the NCVS-1 (screener) and NVCS-2 (crime incident report) instruments to a nationally representative sample of persons age 12 or older living in households in the United States.

The BJS is specifically requesting clearance for the core NCVS from January 2022 through December 2024. The core NCVS includes the administration of the basic screen questionnaire (NCVS-1) and crime incident report (NCVS-2) instruments to a nationally representative sample of persons age 12 or older living in households in the United States, including samples of persons representative of the 22 most populous states in the U.S.

Persons are interviewed on the frequency, characteristics, and consequences of criminal victimization in the United States. The core NCVS survey instrument covers nine general areas: 1) incidence of rape or sexual assault, robbery, aggravated assault, simple assault, personal larceny, burglary, motor vehicle theft, and other theft; 2) characteristics of these victimizations, including location, time, presence of a weapon, injury, and property/monetary loss; 3) characteristics of victims, including sex, age, race, Hispanic origin, disability, and occupation; 4) relationship between victim and offender; 5) emotional impact of victimization; 6) victim self-defense and bystander intervention; 7) offender characteristics including sex, age, race, and Hispanic origin; 8) reporting to police and police response; and 9) bias- or hate-motivated victimizations.

In 2022, the NCVS will have two supplements which will remain in the field for six months. The tentative schedule for the administration of these routine supplements is: January – June, 2022, School Crime Supplement (SCS); July – December, 2022, Police-Public Contact Survey (PPCS). BJS does not plan to administer supplements in 2023-2024. During this period, BJS plans to test and introduce a new instrument.
